title: The Egyptian-Hittite Peace Treaty
text:
Around 1274 BC the armies of Ramesses II of Egypt and the Hittite king Muwatalli II fought a great chariot battle at Kadesh, in Syria. Ramesses was nearly destroyed in an ambush and fought his way out. Both kings claimed victory, and Ramesses covered temple walls with his version. In fact neither side had won, and the struggle for Syria dragged on for years.

About sixteen years later, around 1259 BC, Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III, Muwatalli's brother, concluded a formal peace treaty. It is one of the earliest peace treaties whose text survives from both sides. The Egyptian version was carved in hieroglyphs on temple walls at Karnak and the Ramesseum in Thebes. The Hittite version, written in Akkadian, the diplomatic language of the time, was found on clay tablets in the Hittite capital, Hattusa.

The two kings promised never to attack each other, to come to each other's aid against foreign enemies and rebels, and to hand back fugitives, with a clause requiring that returned fugitives not be punished. Both versions call on the gods of both lands as witnesses.

The peace held for the rest of the Hittite empire's existence. The royal families exchanged letters, and Ramesses later married a Hittite princess. A copy of the treaty is displayed at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
lesson: When neither side can win, the strongest move may be to make the stalemate official and turn a rival into a partner. Both sides can claim honor in peace.
people: Ramesses II, Hattusili III, Muwatalli II
source: The Egyptian text at Karnak and the Ramesseum; the Akkadian tablets from Hattusa
caveat: The exact dates depend on the chronology used for the reign of Ramesses II.
